Eskom: Breaking the Burners

By: Anina Peens | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Insider correspondence and financial statements reveal how Eskom bosses reached deep into the utility’s cookie jar at the expense of the entire South African economy.

Unique Selling Point:
Carte Blanche and News 24 join forces to reveal deep and endemic corruption at Eskom. Hundreds of billions of Rands were blatantly stolen from the state utility, dragging the South African economy to its knees.

Summary:
There are many reasons why South Africa has consistent loadshedding. The biggest blame is the misappropriation of funds that were earmarked to maintain and expand the overburdened underperforming power stations. Instead the funds ended up in the pockets of those in charge. Documents revealing high-level corruption and fraud were anonymously sent to News24, and they shared it with us.

Further information:
Those who were appointed by the ANC government to run and protect Eskom, the lifeline of the South African economy, only had their own interests at heart. For years, they cheated, lied, manipulated and blatantly stole from power utility.
This while power stations that are supposed to carry the South African economy were in urgent need of maintenance and upgrades. Instead, the money availed for maintenance were misappropriated. While the decisionmakers knew the desperate state of the power stations, they drilled the life out of what was left of them. This while personal properties of high-level employees were upgraded and renovated by the same construction companies retained by Eskom. News 24 had anonymously been given hard drives with documents tracing the money that was misappropriated. It reveals secret slush funds that paid out millions in kickbacks and indicate that every single department within Eskom, is corrupt and riddled with fraudulent transactions. One power station that has not received as much attention as Kusile and Medupi, is the Majuba power station near Amersfoort in Mpumalanga. Here, the gravy train is still running in all its glory in the form of fraudulent contracts to black empowerment companies that deliver coal to the country’s second largest power station on a daily basis. This, while Eskom borrowed 4 billion Rand from the world bank in 2010 to build a railway that connects Majuba to collieries in Mpumalanga and Richard’s bay. It has been ten years and 3 billion Rand in additional interest, yet the train is not running. Meanwhile the very lucrative long hauling truck companies are coining from the deliveries and oppose the railway.

Script:


MAJUBA’S WHITE ELEPHANT

UPSOUND:
SUPER@ JOE BIDEN: US PRESIDENT
Today, as part of this commitment, the United States together with the UK, France, Germany and the EU is announcing this partnership with South Africa to help transfer their economy to a clean green economy more quickly.
INTRO
While the Western world wants to help South Africa move away from coal generated electricity, local resistance may be hard to manage. South Africa has massive coal reserves, and a Minister of mining and minerals determined to build more coal fired power stations. And, while Eskom struggles to manage and maintain its existing power stations, it appears the coal industry is keeping the utility on a short leash. Over the past couple of months, Carte Blanche has focussed on Mpumalanga’s Majuba station, the country’s third largest and a serial contributor to blackouts.
STRAP: GWEDE MANTASHE: MINISTER OF MINERAL RESOURCES

CASE STUDY
Scenes like this are common on the road between the town of Amersfoort and the Majuba power station. In 2003, Eskom changed its coal procurement policy to help transform the industry by diversifying supply. Today, various mines scattered across Mpumalanga province sell and deliver coal to Eskom.

LINK
About 1500 trucks deliver coal to the station every day. Many coal transport companies as well as small mines were developed purely for this purpose and an entire eco-system was created and which Eskom has admitted it’s lost control.

VO
Currently, coal sells for roughly R460 Randper tonne. A Truck like this carries at least 30 tonnes, meaning one truck load of coal costs in the region of 13 thousand 800 Rand. Multiply that by 1500 trucks and a back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests Eskom is spending more than 20 million Rand each day to keep Majuba supplied with coal.

VO
Most of Eskom’s power stations are connected to their own coal mines. Majuba also had a mine but it was closed down in 1996.

LINK
This is the original shaft of the mine that was sunk in the 1980’s. The reason given for the mine’s sudden closure was an unforeseen geological fault.

VO
Energy expert Chris Yelland explains that the so called fault was only realised when the station was already under construction.

SUPER@ CHRIS YELLAND:ENERGY EXPERT
CARD 19 OCTOBER
A074C789_211019M2_CANON
8’22’30’12
“...they found that the coal seam underground was very much broken up and could not be mined as continuous coal seam and couldn’t be mined at all. So the whole idea of building this power station next to the mine came to an end.

VO
That means Eskom had a power station but no coal. Its first unit was connected to the grid in 1996 and needed about 8 million tons of coal annually. The solution? Transport coal to the power station by rail, by constructing what’s known as a branch link from Majuba to the station at Palmfort. From there it connected to the existing Durban line.

LINK
This is the old Plamfort line that was built in the 1990’s but cannot meet Majuba’s full demand. Behind me is a tippler system that was built specifically for the Palmfort line. The train wagons would come through and tip the coal onto a conveyor belt.

VO
By 2001, Majuba’s coal needs had increased to 14 million tons per year, substantially more than the Palmford railway line could carry. With trucks making up some of the shortfall, Eskom decided a new railway line was needed to meet total demand. They called it simply “the Majuba” or “Ermelo” line.

SUPER@ CHRIS YELLAND: ENERGY EXPERT
“So, they had to build another line that is coming from the Richards Bay line, 68km from the Richards bay line to Majuba and that could supply 100% of the coal and it was cheaper.
VO
In theory, the Majuba line can supply all 14 million tonnes of coal needed by the power station each year, by linking to the main Richards Bay line which delivers top quality coal for export. The brand new Majuba line is much longer than the Palmfort line as project manager Themba Khumalo explains.

SUPER@ THEMBA KHUMALO: MAJUBA RAILWAY PROJECT
“The Palmfort line comes South of the station as you can see the coal stock yardBut at the end of the Majuba yard we got the new Ermelo line that goes straight across, all the way to Ermelo.

VO

Construction of the 68km Majuba railway started in 2011.
It’s now a decade later and the line is a vandalized white elephant.
Eskom said the Majuba line would be fully operational by 2020. But, then December 2019 sabotage was investigated after the conveyor belt burnt down.

LINK
This is the conveyor belt that moves the coal from the tippler to the boilers and right here, in 2019, is where it mysteriously burnt down.

The conveyor belt connects the tippler system situated on the railway to the boilers.
The tippler was built when the Palmfort line was built in 1996 but the Majuba line can also use it to offload its wagons.

VO
Now, because a fully operational Majuba line is capable of meeting the power station’s entire annual coal requirement, trucking businesses are under threat.

SUPER@ CHRIS YELLAND: ENERGY EXPERT
“They rely on the ongoing success of this business otherwise they go bankrupt. And this created a kind of momentum that is very hard to stop. And in fact, there is massive resistance if you try and stop this process.”

MASA INTERACTION WITH TRUCK DRIVER ZULU TRANSLATION. PLEASE BLUR FACE AND SUBTITLE
Clip (A090C877_211109CI_CANON_01)
00:16-00:19
Masa: So, if this railway would work, how would this affect you?
00:21-00:00:23
Driver: The trucks will have to stop working.
00:24-00:25
Masa: What does it mean to you?
00:25-00:27
Driver: We will starve.

VO
In a wide-ranging interview last month, Eskom CEO, Andre De Ruyter, repeated that the utility had in the past lost control of the quality of coal delivered by road.

SUPER@ANDRE DE RUYTER: ESKOM CEO SOCIAL
“On route, trucks were relieved of some of the coal that they carried, they were filled with water or with metal to get the weight right and this mixture which obviously does not burn so well was then deposited at our power stations and it caused damage to the power stations.”

VO
De Ruyter says Eskom now insists the trucks are properly sealed. If the delivered coal is mixed with rubble to increase weight and - therefore - payment it can damage the boilers that generate the steam needed to make electricity. Prof Willie Cronje is from the WITS School of Electrical Engineering explains that the power stations were not designed to burn a fruit salad of different grades of coal.

SUPER@PROF WILLIE CRONJÉ: ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING: WITS
“They can overheat and burst. That is basically when the steam comes out. They can also build up slack around them if your coal is not of the right grade. You actually get slack build up and you don’t get enough power out of the system as you like to. What we need to understand is that every power station is optimized the furnace, for a specific grade of coal.

VO
Each time the tubes inside the boilers break, the unit is switched off, cooled down, fixed and started up again - with blackouts the inevitable outcome. But, what if the Majuba railway line was up and running? Would Eskom regain control of its coal supply? During his interview, De Ruyter assured us trains were running.

SUPER@ANDRE DE RUYTER: ESKOM CEO
“So, we have just in the past week seen the railway tippler that we have installed to enable us to reduce the number of trucks on the road form 1400 per day to less than 200 a day. That railway tippler was finally commissioned after extensive delays caused by procurement amongst other things. And we are now in a position where we can again transport coal by rail to Majuba”

MASA: And how soon will that be?

SUPER@ANDRE DE RUYTER: ESKOM CEO
That is happening right now.

MASA: So, that railway line is actually active right now?

SUPER@ANDRE DE RUYTER: ESKOM CEO
Correct.

VO

But, De Ruyter is referring to the old Palmfort line - deemed inadequate back in 2001 - and couldn’t say when the Majuba line will be operational. On two recent visits to the power station, no coal was being delivered by rail, not even on the old Palmfort line. The tippler off-loading system was only switched on for us to film. Back at Eskom, we sought answers from senior project manager Thulani Mtshali

SUPER@THULANI MTSHALI: SNR.MANAGER: CAPITAL PROJECTS: ESKOM
9’55’54’24
“Most of the work has been done. Apart from the issues that we have had to deal with of theft and vandalism that has happened in the last two or three years of infrastructure, completed infrastructure by the way. The 68km line is complete to the extent that by the end of November this year we should be able to come back on the Palmfort line and at the minimum run treat three trains a day to supply coal to Majuba.

VO
But Mtshali is also referring to the older Palmfort line. It would seem there’s a reluctance to address the white elephant in the room: When will the Majuba line begin operating, allowing Eskom greater control of coal supply and likely avoiding further damage to the power station? Mtshali did have a view on the second part of that question, saying there’s no link between the supply of coal via road and the performance of the power station.

SUPER@THULANI MTSHALI: SNR.MANAGER: CAPITAL PROJECTS: ESKOM
10’13’28’13
“There is no constraint as a result of coal not being moved by rail there is no constraint regarding the productivity of the station. There is direct link to loadshedding as a result of Majuba as far as I am aware.”

VO
In a written reply Eskom said a unit was shut down at Majuba beginning November because of a leak in a boiler tube. This was the same week in which Mtshali was interviewed and South Africa experienced extended blackouts.
Majuba is a good example of how the coal industry can determine the direction of a utility as large as Eskom, seemingly with little counter resistance. Even while the world is trying to assist South Africa in clearing its heavy carbon footprint, cutting the lifeline for coal operators can have devastating effects.
x





PROMOS

PROMO 1 21”
This is the Majuba power station where hundreds of trucks deliver coal every day. [big pause]
But this could all come to an end if Majuba's multi-million Rand railway line is fully operational, threatening the livelihoods of many.
ZULU INTERACTION
Clip (A090C877_211109CI_CANON_01)
00:06-00:11
Masa: if this railway should work how would you feel about that, because the trucks won’t be needed anymore?
00:21-00:00:23
Driver: The trucks will have to stop working.
00:24-00:25
Masa: What does it mean to you?
00:25-00:27
Driver: We will starve.

PROMO 2 21”
Is Eskom taking control over its coal supply chain, or are coal suppliers in charge?
ANDRE DE RUYTER
14”
We are not unsympathetic to the entrepreneurs who have invested in this but from an Eskom perspective we have a duty to the country to ensure that we deliver coal at the lowest possible cost.

PROMOS 11”

2. Coal is a big business, and supplying to Eskom means big bucks. But with a multi-million rand railway line built specifically to transport coal to Majuba power station, why are hundreds of trucks still queuing to make deliveries by road?

3. Majuba[beat].. with a new multi-billion rand railway line, it should be one of Eskom's most efficient power stations. But as hundreds of trucks transport coal, why has the railway become a white elephant?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Insider correspondence and financial statements reveal how Eskom bosses reached deep into the utility’s cookie jar at the expense of the entire South African economy.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Carte Blanche and News 24 join forces to reveal deep and endemic corruption at Eskom. Hundreds of billions of Rands were blatantly stolen from the state utility, dragging the South African economy to its knees.
metadata.Summary: There are many reasons why South Africa has consistent loadshedding. The biggest blame is the misappropriation of funds that were earmarked to maintain and expand the overburdened underperforming power stations. Instead the funds ended up in the pockets of those in charge. Documents revealing high-level corruption and fraud were anonymously sent to News24, and they shared it with us.
metadata.Further information: Those who were appointed by the ANC government to run and protect Eskom, the lifeline of the South African economy, only had their own interests at heart. For years, they cheated, lied, manipulated and blatantly stole from power utility. This while power stations that are supposed to carry the South African economy were in urgent need of maintenance and upgrades. Instead, the money availed for maintenance were misappropriated. While the decisionmakers knew the desperate state of the power stations, they drilled the life out of what was left of them. This while personal properties of high-level employees were upgraded and renovated by the same construction companies retained by Eskom. News 24 had anonymously been given hard drives with documents tracing the money that was misappropriated. It reveals secret slush funds that paid out millions in kickbacks and indicate that every single department within Eskom, is corrupt and riddled with fraudulent transactions. One power station that has not received as much attention as Kusile and Medupi, is the Majuba power station near Amersfoort in Mpumalanga. Here, the gravy train is still running in all its glory in the form of fraudulent contracts to black empowerment companies that deliver coal to the country’s second largest power station on a daily basis. This, while Eskom borrowed 4 billion Rand from the world bank in 2010 to build a railway that connects Majuba to collieries in Mpumalanga and Richard’s bay. It has been ten years and 3 billion Rand in additional interest, yet the train is not running. Meanwhile the very lucrative long hauling truck companies are coining from the deliveries and oppose the railway.
